overview: A method is a function with a special receiver parameter that binds the function to a named type, written `func (r Receiver) Name(params) results`.
Go lets you define methods on any named (defined) type in the same package — not just structs — so `type Celsius float64` can have a `String()` method too.

The receiver comes in two flavors, value (`func (t T) M()`) and pointer (`func (t *T) M()`); the choice controls whether the method sees a copy or the original, and which method set the type exposes for interface satisfaction.
learningObjectives: Declare methods with both value and pointer receivers and explain the difference in behavior.
State the method set rules and predict when `T` versus `*T` satisfies an interface.
Use method values (`t.M`) and method expressions (`T.M` / `(*T).M`) and explain how they bind the receiver.
Apply receiver naming and value-vs-pointer conventions, and reason about nil pointer receivers and large-value copy cost.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A method is a function declared with a receiver, a parameter that appears between the `func` keyword and the method name and associates the function with the receiver's base type; method invocation `x.M(args)` is syntactic sugar that passes `x` as the receiver argument.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: A method is just a function that 'belongs to' a type. You write the type it belongs to in parentheses before the name. If you write that type as a value, the method gets its own copy; if you write it as a pointer (`*T`), the method can change the original.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Go deliberately omits classes and inheritance. Instead of attaching behavior inside a class body, the designers (Pike, Thompson, Griesemer) chose free-standing method declarations that can be attached to any defined type in the declaring package. This decision, present since Go's 2009 release, lets behavior and data live separately and makes interface satisfaction structural and implicit rather than declared.

whyItMatters.business: Methods are how Go models domain behavior (an `Order.Total()`, an `Account.Withdraw()`), giving teams a clean, discoverable API surface that maps directly to business rules.
whyItMatters.engineering: Correct receiver choice prevents an entire class of silent bugs where mutations 'disappear' because they were applied to a copy.
whyItMatters.scalability: Methods plus interfaces enable structural polymorphism, so large codebases can swap implementations (mock vs real DB) without touching call sites.
whyItMatters.cost: Choosing pointer receivers for large structs avoids copying kilobytes per call, reducing CPU and allocation overhead in hot paths.
whyItMatters.reliability: Understanding method sets prevents the common 'does not implement interface (method has pointer receiver)' compile error and the runtime surprises of mutating copies.

coreComponents.name: Receiver
coreComponents.definition: The parameter declared in parentheses before the method name that binds the method to a type.
coreComponents.purpose: Associate behavior with a specific named type and give the method access to that instance.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Name the instance (conventionally a short, consistent identifier) and declare whether the method operates on a value (T) or pointer (*T).
coreComponents.examples: func (c Counter) Value() int — `c` is the receiver

coreComponents.name: Value receiver
coreComponents.definition: A receiver declared as `func (t T) M()` that receives a copy of the value.
coreComponents.purpose: Read or compute from the instance without mutating the original.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Operate on an independent copy; any changes are discarded after the call.

coreComponents.name: Pointer receiver
coreComponents.definition: A receiver declared as `func (t *T) M()` that receives the address of the value.
coreComponents.purpose: Mutate the original instance or avoid copying a large struct.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Modify fields in place and expose the method in *T's method set.

coreComponents.name: Method set
coreComponents.definition: The set of methods callable on a given type T or *T, which determines interface satisfaction.
coreComponents.purpose: Define which interfaces a value or pointer satisfies.
coreComponents.responsibilities: T's set holds value-receiver methods; *T's set holds both value- and pointer-receiver methods.
coreComponents.examples: Only *Buffer satisfies io.Writer if Write has a pointer receiver

coreComponents.name: Method value
coreComponents.definition: An expression `t.M` that yields a function with the receiver already bound to `t`.
coreComponents.purpose: Capture a method together with its receiver as a first-class function.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Evaluate and bind the receiver at the moment the method value is created.

coreComponents.name: Method expression
coreComponents.definition: An expression `T.M` or `(*T).M` that yields a function whose first parameter is the explicit receiver.
coreComponents.purpose: Get an unbound function so the receiver is passed as an argument.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Produce func(T, params) (results) or func(*T, params) (results).

internalWorking: The compiler rewrites a method declaration `func (t T) M(a int)` into something equivalent to a function `M(t T, a int)`; the call `x.M(3)` is rewritten to pass `x` (or `&x`) as the first argument.
For a value receiver, the call copies the receiver onto the stack just like any by-value parameter; mutations affect only that copy.
For a pointer receiver, the call passes the address, so the method dereferences and operates on the original storage.

When you call `t.M()` and M has a pointer receiver but `t` is an addressable value, the compiler automatically inserts `(&t).M()`; when M has a value receiver and `t` is a pointer, it inserts `(*t).M()`.

This auto-address/auto-deref convenience only applies to direct calls on addressable operands. For interface satisfaction the method set is computed strictly: a value of type T does NOT include pointer-receiver methods, so it cannot satisfy an interface that requires them.
Method values capture the receiver immediately and store it in a closure-like value; method expressions produce a plain function that takes the receiver explicitly.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: source: func (t *T) M() --> compiler binds M to base type T --> call x.M() --> [is x addressable? auto &x or *x as needed] --> pass receiver arg --> method body runs on value-copy (T) or original (*T) --> for interface assignment: check method set of static type (T vs *T) strictly
dataFlowWalkthrough: You declare `type Counter struct{ n int }` and `func (c *Counter) Inc() { c.n++ }`.
You write `c.Inc()`; because Inc needs *Counter and `c` is addressable, the compiler rewrites this to `(&c).Inc()`.
Inside Inc, `c` is the address of the original, so `c.n++` increments the real variable.

If instead you tried to assign `c` (a Counter value) to an interface that requires Inc, it would fail to compile, because Counter's method set does not include pointer-receiver methods — only *Counter's does.

keyTerminology.meaning: The bound instance parameter of a method.
keyTerminology.importance: It is what distinguishes a method from a plain function.

keyTerminology.meaning: The collection of methods a type exposes; T has value-receiver methods, *T has both.
keyTerminology.importance: Determines which interfaces a type satisfies.

keyTerminology.meaning: Whether an operand has a memory address (variables, slice elements, dereferenced pointers are addressable; map elements and literals generally are not).
keyTerminology.importance: Controls whether the compiler can auto-take-address to call a pointer-receiver method.

keyTerminology.meaning: `t.M` — a function with the receiver already bound.
keyTerminology.importance: Lets you pass a method+receiver as a callback.

keyTerminology.meaning: `T.M` — a function taking the receiver as its first explicit argument.
keyTerminology.importance: Useful for generic dispatch and higher-order programming.

keyTerminology.meaning: A type created with a `type` declaration, e.g. `type Celsius float64`.
keyTerminology.importance: Methods can only be declared on defined types in the same package, not on built-ins or aliases of other packages.

importantConcepts.explanation: A value receiver gets a copy, so any field assignment is lost when the method returns. To change the original you must use `*T`.

If a method has a pointer receiver, only `*T` is in the interface-satisfying method set. A `T` value (or a `T` stored in a map, which is not addressable) cannot satisfy that interface even though `t.M()` compiles for an addressable variable.
Idiomatic Go uses the same receiver kind (all pointer or all value) across a type's methods. Mixing them is confusing and can cause unexpected method-set gaps.
A method with a pointer receiver can be called on a nil pointer as long as the body doesn't dereference nil; this is used for things like a nil *TreeNode representing an empty tree.

importantConcepts.concept: You can declare methods on any defined type
importantConcepts.explanation: Named slice, map, function, and numeric types can all have methods, which is how `type Celsius float64` gets `String()` or `type IntSlice []int` gets `Sort()`.

variationsAndTypes: Value-receiver methods (read-only / small immutable types like Point or time.Time).
Pointer-receiver methods (mutating methods or large structs).
Methods on named non-struct types (e.g. `type Celsius float64`, `type Handler func(...)`).
Methods that implement standard interfaces (Stringer, error, io.Writer, sort.Interface).
Nil-safe pointer-receiver methods (linked lists, trees, optional state).
Promoted methods from embedded types (the outer type gains the embedded type's methods).
advantages: Attaches behavior to data cleanly without classes or inheritance.
Enables structural interface satisfaction — a type implements an interface just by having the right methods.
Pointer receivers allow efficient in-place mutation and avoid copying large structs.
Methods on named primitives let you add domain meaning and formatting (Celsius.String()).
Method values and expressions make methods first-class for callbacks and dispatch.
disadvantages: The value-vs-pointer choice is a frequent source of subtle bugs (mutating a copy).
Method-set rules cause the confusing 'does not implement interface' compile errors.
Value receivers on large structs copy data on every call, hurting performance.
Mixing receiver kinds on one type leads to inconsistent method sets.
Methods can only be defined in the type's own package, limiting extension of foreign types.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use a pointer receiver when the method mutates the receiver, when the struct is large, or to keep the type's receivers consistent. Use a value receiver for small, immutable types (numbers, small structs) where copying is cheap and you want value semantics.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid a value receiver when you intend to mutate state or when the type is large; avoid a pointer receiver for tiny immutable types where it adds indirection and prevents convenient use as map keys or constants.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of a method as an instruction printed on an item's manual that says 'do X to this item.' A value receiver is like handing someone a photocopy of the item to scribble on — the original is untouched. A pointer receiver is like giving them the item's locker key — changes apply to the real thing. The method set is the list of operations the front desk will accept depending on whether you bring the item itself or its locker key.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Methods can only be defined on structs.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Any defined type in the same package can have methods, including named slices, maps, functions, and numeric types like `type Celsius float64`.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Calling a value-receiver method through a pointer mutates the original.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go auto-dereferences the pointer, but the method still operates on a copy of the pointed-to value, so mutations are lost.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If `t.M()` compiles for a value, then a `T` value satisfies any interface containing M.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Auto-addressing makes the call compile for an addressable variable, but interface satisfaction uses the strict method set; a pointer-receiver M means only *T satisfies the interface.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Calling a method on a nil pointer always panics.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It only panics if the body dereferences the nil pointer; a well-written pointer-receiver method can handle a nil receiver gracefully.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Prefer pointer receivers for large structs so high-throughput code paths don't copy big values on every method call.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Keep receiver kinds consistent per type to avoid method-set surprises that break interface assignments at refactor time.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Design pointer-receiver methods to tolerate a nil receiver where a nil instance is a legitimate state (empty tree/list).
productionConsiderations.monitoring: There is nothing runtime-specific to monitor for methods themselves; profile hot methods with pprof to catch expensive value-receiver copies.
productionConsiderations.security: Be careful exposing pointer-receiver methods that mutate shared state across goroutines; protect with synchronization since the receiver aliases the original.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Avoid unnecessary value-receiver copies of large structs; benchmark with `go test -bench` and inspect escape analysis with `-gcflags=-m`.
productionConsiderations.performance: Method dispatch on concrete types is a direct call (cheap); calls through an interface incur an indirect dispatch and may cause the receiver to escape to the heap.

codeExamples.title: Value receiver vs pointer receiver: who gets mutated
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrate that a value-receiver method mutates only a copy while a pointer-receiver method mutates the original.
codeExamples.breakdown: IncValue receives a copy of Counter, so `c.n++` increments that copy and the change vanishes when the method returns. IncPointer receives `*Counter`, so it mutates the original. Because `c` is an addressable variable, `c.IncPointer()` is automatically rewritten to `(&c).IncPointer()`. The final call through the explicit pointer `p` mutates the same underlying Counter.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
after IncValue: 0
after IncPointer: 1
after p.IncPointer: 2
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting IncValue to change c; forgetting that map elements and literals are not addressable, so you cannot call a pointer-receiver method on them directly (e.g. `m["k"].IncPointer()` won't compile).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For mutation or large structs, default to pointer receivers; keep all of a type's receivers the same kind for consistency.

codeExamples.title: Method sets and interface satisfaction with pointer receivers
codeExamples.overview: Show that when a method has a pointer receiver, only *T satisfies the interface — not a T value.
codeExamples.breakdown: String() has a pointer receiver, so it lives only in *Temp's method set. The direct call `t.String()` compiles because `t` is addressable and Go inserts the address-of. But interface assignment is strict: `var s Stringer = &t` works while `var s Stringer = t` does not, because the Temp value's method set lacks String(). Storing pointers in the map keeps them usable.
codeExamples.commonIssues: The classic 'X does not implement I (method has pointer receiver)' error when you assign a value instead of a pointer; trying to call a pointer-receiver method on a non-addressable map value.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If you want both T and *T to satisfy an interface, use a value receiver (its method is in both method sets). Choose pointer receivers when mutation or copy-cost matters and pass *T to interfaces.

codeExamples.title: Method values vs method expressions on a named numeric type
codeExamples.overview: Define a method on a non-struct named type and contrast a bound method value with an unbound method expression.
codeExamples.breakdown: Celsius is a defined type over float64 and can carry the Fahrenheit method. `boiling.Fahrenheit` is a method VALUE: it captures `boiling` immediately and yields a `func() float64`. `Celsius.Fahrenheit` is a method EXPRESSION: it yields `func(Celsius) float64`, taking the receiver explicitly, so you can apply it to any Celsius value. This is how methods become first-class for callbacks and dispatch.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
method value: 212
method expression: 32
method expression: 212
codeExamples.commonIssues: Confusing the two forms; a method value snapshots the receiver at creation time, so later changes to the variable are not reflected in an already-captured value receiver.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use method values for callbacks where the receiver is fixed (e.g. registering `obj.Handle` as a handler); use method expressions when you need to apply the same method across many receivers.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A billing service needs a Money type that formats correctly, supports addition, and can be used wherever the standard fmt.Stringer interface is expected, while avoiding silent rounding and mutation bugs.
endToEndExample.inputData: Amounts in integer cents (e.g. 1999 for $19.99) wrapped in a defined type `type Money int64`.
endToEndExample.architecture: A named numeric type Money with a value-receiver String() for formatting and a value-receiver Add() returning a new Money (value semantics, immutable), implementing fmt.Stringer so it prints correctly anywhere.
processingSteps: Define `type Money int64` so cents carry domain meaning and methods.
Add `func (m Money) String() string` (value receiver) to format as currency; this puts String() in both Money and *Money method sets.
Add `func (m Money) Add(o Money) Money` returning a new value to preserve immutability.
Assign a Money value to fmt.Stringer to confirm interface satisfaction with a value receiver.
Print and sum amounts, observing that originals are never mutated.
endToEndExample.output: Formatted currency strings like "$19.99" and a correct sum without mutating inputs.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Profile formatting on hot reporting paths; ensure String() does not allocate excessively under load.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Because Money is an integer type, there is no floating-point rounding error; guard against overflow on Add for extreme values if needed.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A clean, interface-satisfying value type where the value-receiver choice gives safe immutable semantics and lets both Money and *Money be used as fmt.Stringer.

industryUseCases.problem: Modeling many resource types that must render and validate themselves uniformly.
industryUseCases.solution: Defined types implement shared interfaces via methods with carefully chosen pointer receivers so providers can mutate and finalize resource state in place.
industryUseCases.benefits: Pluggable providers satisfy interfaces structurally, and pointer receivers avoid copying large config structs.

industryUseCases.problem: Representing money and currency safely without floating-point bugs.
industryUseCases.solution: Named integer types (e.g. Money) with value-receiver methods like String() and Add() that implement fmt.Stringer and preserve value/immutable semantics.
industryUseCases.benefits: Domain-correct formatting, no accidental mutation, and the type works anywhere a Stringer is accepted.

industryUseCases.problem: Large API objects (Pods, Deployments) need methods to mutate and DeepCopy state efficiently.
industryUseCases.solution: Methods use pointer receivers consistently on big structs so mutations apply to the real object and avoid kilobyte-scale copies per call.
industryUseCases.benefits: Correct in-place updates and lower CPU/allocation cost across high-frequency controller loops.

productionDeepDive.scalability: On large structs in high-QPS paths, pointer receivers avoid per-call copies; this is the difference between copying a few bytes (a pointer) and copying an entire object on every method invocation.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Pointer-receiver methods can be made nil-safe (check `if t == nil`) so a nil instance is a valid, handled state rather than a panic — common for tree/list nodes.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Keeping receiver kinds consistent prevents refactor-time breakage where switching a method to a pointer receiver suddenly removes a type from an interface's method set and breaks builds across services.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Value-receiver methods that return new values (immutable style) make state easy to snapshot and replay because methods never mutate inputs unexpectedly.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Inspect escape analysis with `go build -gcflags=-m`; calling methods through interfaces can force the receiver to escape to the heap, so prefer concrete types on the hottest paths and benchmark before changing receiver kinds.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Right-size receivers: pointer receivers for big structs cut allocation/copy CPU, while value receivers for tiny types avoid pointer indirection and keep data on the stack.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Because a pointer receiver aliases the original, a pointer-receiver method invoked concurrently can race on shared state; guard mutating methods with a mutex or confine the instance to one goroutine.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use pprof CPU and alloc profiles to spot expensive value-receiver copies and interface-dispatch hotspots; there is no special method-level metric beyond standard profiling.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Put validation in pointer-receiver mutating methods (e.g. Setters) so invariants are enforced in one place rather than scattered across callers.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Implement String() / error methods on domain types so logs render meaningful, consistent representations; ensure these methods are cheap and side-effect free so logging never alters state.

recommendedPractices: Use a pointer receiver when the method mutates the receiver or the struct is large.
Use a value receiver for small, immutable types where copying is cheap (numbers, small structs).
Keep all of a single type's receivers the same kind (all pointer or all value) for a consistent method set.
Make pointer-receiver methods nil-safe when a nil receiver is a legitimate state.
engineeringStandards: When in doubt for structs, default to pointer receivers (matches Kubernetes/std-lib practice for non-trivial types).
Assign pointers (*T) to interfaces when the type uses pointer receivers to satisfy the strict method set.
Don't define methods that mutate state on value receivers — it silently fails.
designRecommendations: Define methods on named primitive types (Celsius, Duration) to add domain meaning and formatting.
Implement standard interfaces (Stringer, error, sort.Interface) where it improves ergonomics.
Prefer returning new values from methods on small immutable types instead of mutating.
namingConventions: Use a short, consistent receiver name (one or two letters derived from the type, e.g. `c` for Counter, `t` for Temp).
Never name the receiver `this` or `self`; Go convention is a short abbreviation of the type.
Use the same receiver name across all methods of a type.
documentationStandards: Document whether a method mutates the receiver (especially for pointer receivers).
Note in godoc when a method is safe to call on a nil pointer receiver.
Document which interfaces a type implements via its methods.
testingStrategies: Test that pointer-receiver methods actually mutate and value-receiver methods do not.
Add a compile-time assertion `var _ Interface = (*T)(nil)` to verify interface satisfaction.
Benchmark large-struct methods to confirm pointer receivers avoid copy cost.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a value receiver for a method intended to mutate state.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Forgetting the receiver is a copy.
commonMistakes.impact: Mutations are silently discarded; the bug is hard to spot.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a pointer receiver `func (t *T) M()` for any mutating method.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assigning a value to an interface when the method has a pointer receiver.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Auto-addressing makes direct calls compile, masking the method-set rule.
commonMistakes.impact: Compile error: 'X does not implement I (method has pointer receiver)'.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Assign a pointer (&x) to the interface, or use value receivers if you need both T and *T to satisfy it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a pointer-receiver method on a non-addressable value (e.g. a map element).
commonMistakes.impact: Compile error: 'cannot call pointer method on m[key]'.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Store pointers in the map, or copy to an addressable local variable first.

commonMistakes.impact: Non-idiomatic code flagged by linters and reviewers.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a short, consistent abbreviation of the type name.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing value and pointer receivers on the same type.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Adding methods over time without a convention.
commonMistakes.impact: Inconsistent method set causes surprising interface-satisfaction gaps.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Pick one receiver kind per type and apply it to all its methods.

comparisonSection.explanation: Value receivers operate on a copy and cannot mutate the original; pointer receivers mutate it in place.

comparisonSection.optionA: Value receiver — in both T and *T sets
comparisonSection.explanation: A pointer-receiver method means only *T satisfies an interface; a value-receiver method lets both T and *T satisfy it.

comparisonSection.optionA: Value receiver copies the whole value
comparisonSection.optionB: Pointer receiver copies only a pointer
comparisonSection.explanation: For large structs, value receivers can be expensive; pointer receivers pass an address regardless of size.
A method binds to a type and participates in method sets/interfaces and dot-call syntax; a plain function does not and cannot satisfy interfaces.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the syntax for declaring a method in Go?
beginnerQuestions.answer: `func (r ReceiverType) Name(params) results { ... }` — the receiver appears in parentheses before the method name.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tests the basic distinction between a method and a function.

beginnerQuestions.question: Can you define a method on a non-struct type?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Yes — on any defined type in the same package, such as `type Celsius float64` with a method `func (c Celsius) Fahrenheit() float64`.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Checks that the student knows methods are not limited to structs.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between a value receiver and a pointer receiver?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A value receiver gets a copy and cannot mutate the original; a pointer receiver gets the address and can mutate it. Pointer receivers also avoid copying large structs.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Core to writing correct, efficient methods.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why does `t.M()` compile but `var i Iface = t` fail when M has a pointer receiver?
intermediateQuestions.answer: For a direct call on an addressable variable the compiler auto-takes the address (`(&t).M()`). Interface satisfaction uses the strict method set, and a pointer-receiver method is only in *T's set, so the value t doesn't satisfy the interface.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding of addressability versus method sets.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the difference between a method value and a method expression.
advancedQuestions.answer: A method value `t.M` binds the receiver now and yields `func(params) results`. A method expression `T.M` yields `func(T, params) results`, taking the receiver explicitly. `(*T).M` does the same for pointer receivers.

advancedQuestions.question: When is it safe to call a method on a nil pointer receiver?
advancedQuestions.answer: When the method body does not dereference the nil receiver — e.g. it checks `if t == nil` and returns a sensible default. This pattern is used for empty trees/lists.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests deeper knowledge of pointer-receiver semantics.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A teammate's UpdateName method on a User struct 'doesn't work' — the name never changes after calling it.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: A method that fails to mutate almost always has a value receiver, so it edits a copy. Check the receiver type.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Change `func (u User) UpdateName(...)` to a pointer receiver `func (u *User) UpdateName(...)` so it mutates the original; ensure callers hold an addressable User or a *User.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a plugin system where many concrete types implement a common Renderer interface, some needing internal mutation during render.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Define the Renderer interface; implement it with pointer receivers on the concrete types so they can mutate internal caches, and store *T instances in the registry so they satisfy the interface.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Pointer receivers mean only *T satisfies Renderer and the instances are shared/aliased, so concurrent rendering needs synchronization; value receivers would allow both T and *T but forbid mutation.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Pool reusable renderer instances, keep receivers consistent, and benchmark interface-dispatch hot paths; shard work across goroutines while ensuring each instance is used by one goroutine at a time.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A method is a function with a receiver that binds it to a named type; receivers are value (copy) or pointer (original).
keyConcepts: Syntax: func (r T) Name(...) / func (r *T) Name(...).
Pointer receiver to mutate or for large structs; value receiver for small immutable types.
Method set: T has value methods; *T has both value and pointer methods.
Methods can be defined on any defined type in the same package, not just structs.
formulas: interface satisfied(I, T) ⇔ methods(I) ⊆ methodSet(T); methodSet(*T) ⊇ methodSet(T)
commands: go vet ./...                      # flags some receiver/copy issues
go build -gcflags=-m             # escape analysis for receiver copies
interviewPoints: Value receiver = copy, cannot mutate; pointer receiver = original.
Pointer-receiver method ⇒ only *T satisfies the interface.
Auto-address for direct calls ≠ method set for interfaces.
Receiver name: short, consistent, never this/self.
quickNotes: Method value t.M binds receiver now; method expression T.M takes it as an argument.
Nil pointer receivers are fine if the body doesn't dereference nil.
Map elements and literals are not addressable — pointer methods need addressable operands.
Keep receiver kinds consistent across a type's methods.

keyTakeaways: A method is a function with a receiver written `func (r T) Name(...)`; the receiver can be a value (copy) or a pointer (original).
Use pointer receivers to mutate the receiver or to avoid copying large structs; use value receivers for small immutable types, and keep the kind consistent per type.
Method sets drive interface satisfaction: a pointer-receiver method puts the method only in *T's set, so only *T satisfies the interface even though auto-addressing makes direct calls compile.
Methods work on any defined type (e.g. `type Celsius float64`), nil pointer receivers can be valid, and `t.M` (method value) versus `T.M` (method expression) makes methods first-class.
